​Since it looks like Dell is preventing people to write real reviews on products, here is mine, after one month about of usage of my new Dell Inspiron G5 15 5500.​
​Dell Inspiron G5 15 5500 (​​CPU i7-10750H, GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2070 8GB, RAM 16GB DDR4-2933MHz, SSD 1TB M.2 PCIe NVMe​​)​
​A month ago I bought the new Dell Inspiron G5 15 5500 and have been using it for a while. Certainly it is very fast, thanks also to the SSD and the new generation CPU, but I was still very disappointed, especially considering that it is a machine that costs 1800.00 EUR in the configuration I bought. There are several reasons:​
​1. THE BATTERY LIFE​​Using the laptop normally for surfing, without launching heavy applications and even less graphical ones or games, the laptop dropped from 100% charge to just 6% in an hour and 42 minutes. Simply ridiculous. I have checked the battery with the Dell Power Battery Manager and it is in very good health: the 10 hours that Dell is proclaiming are far from reality.​​2. THE NOISE OF THE FANS​​Even when the laptop is doing nothing, fans run at full blast even if the room temperature is low. The noise is really excessive, so much so that it is difficult to concentrate, also because I use it for work and not for play.​​3. THE POWER SUPPLY​​At times it weighs more than the laptop and is huge, certainly not portable. Dell's website says «now you can quickly recharge your system with a 51 or 68 Wh battery.» On the one supplied there are the W's, not the Wh's, and it is 240W. However, the connector is proprietary so it is not clear if I can buy a lighter compatible power supply to take with me and leave the original one at home. In any case, on the Dell website the power supplies are not to be purchased separately.​​4. THE DELL DOCKING STATION​​When I asked Dell which specific Docking Station I should use for this machine, they replied that this laptop is not compatible with any Dell Docking Station, except the Universal one, which also works in theory with any laptop, even non-Dell and that, look case, it is the most expensive.​​5. THE RTX 2070 GPU​​If the laptop is connected to one or two monitors via ANY Docking Station, it does NOT use the NVidia card but the integrated Intel one, too little powerful to work seriously with graphics applications. The only way to use the RTX 2070's GPU is to connect the primary monitor directly to the laptop, which reduces the usefulness of having a docking station. When I called Dell Support, it was the only suggestion they gave. Disappointing.​​6. THE NETWORK CARD​​For some mysterious reason it cannot see what WiFi networks are there, even if Discovery Network is enabled for the network profile I use. However, if one manually specify the SSID and password of the network, the laptop finds it. Which means the card works, but it can't automatically find networks.​​7. THE SOFTWARE​​Windows 10 Pro is really unstable on this machine. Whether it's the laptop or Windows's fault is hard to say. The Microsoft Store does NOT work and consequently none of the Apps, so much so that I had to install Open-Shell in order to use the Start button. None of the many methods easily found on the net to restore the Store work. I have also installed several Dell Apps, such as the Alienware Control Center and the Dell Power Manager. If you run after installation they work, but since they probably only create a tile in the Start Menu and not an icon on the desktop, after closing them, I can't run them anymore.​
​To conclude, a powerful and expensive machine that creates many expectations but does not satisfy them. I honestly don't recommend it.​

Titulo_Post: Inspiron G5 15-5587, thermals, cooling, fan control
Conteudo_Post:
​Before you read: ​​This is a recap of what I've seen on the forums and I want you to use it as a post for information, this is by no mean a tutorial to tweak your computer, the things I list below are here only for informing other G series owners of what the situation is now. I didn't test anything that stated "this could impact on hardware lifetime" or anything similar.​
​I've got my G5 5 days ago, it's rocking an i7 8750h and an Nvidia 1050ti with 16Gb of ram and all the other irrelevant stuff.​
​I updated BIOS to 1.5.0 with all the other stuff prompted from the Dell support center and found out how bad the fan curves are. Worst of all, a user can't really access any kind of control by default, they're just like that. "Thermal cooling" is even sponsored on the sticker on the chassis. 1.4.1 seems to be the same.​
​ ​

​ ​
​ ​
​ ​
​ ​
​ ​
​ ​
​ ​
​ ​
​ ​
​Now: I'm kind of fixed on thermals and I love to have full control and monitoring on my hardware, I have another macBook Pro which has a custom fan curve (macsFan) on both MacOS and Windows Bootcamp, and a desktop computer with an i7 6700 in a MINI ITX case THAT NEVER REACHED +75 degrees in the heaviest of stress tests paired with an overclocked nvidia GTX 970.​
​My heart almost broke when I saw 92° on a cpu core on HWMonitor after booting a game to test thermals (Dark Souls 3, Medium Settings, 1080p locked at 60fps).​
​I have bought this G5 instead of a 100 euro cheaper G3 with the same exact specs because of the beefier cooler because I want my computers to last for years (my macbook is still 100% ok, even battery, after 8 years being my daily driver, and note that I use my daily driver 12 hours a day at least, 24/7).​
​Now, I did some testing, I'm positive ​​it's all because of the fans curve, they kick in too late, ​​right after they get to the right speed, the computer gets way cooler, but the temperature spikes between the clock ramp and the fans activating are probably dangerous on computer components in the long run and I don't like my left hand sweating just because the fans are not spinning.​
​Please don't say that having fans spinning more frequently than this would damage the pc, I prefer to get faster consuption on my fans to replace them in 2-3 years for 30 euro instead of replacing my m.2 drive or my motherboard.​
​In fact, after the fans start spinning, everything gets kind of cool (mid 70°s under gaming/working load).​
​The problem is how long they take to act, this is not only a problem at boot, since they sometimes slow down because of a change of scene or something momentarily lighter on cpu/GPU to get again super hot and start spinning again, resulting in thermal throttle and all those bad things.​
​Reading other posts, I understand that Dell is not the direct producer for the motherboards and this slow reaction to this problem (take a look at the forum, posts on fan curves and thermals are all over the place) might be caused by some uneffective communication between companies. What we know is that we don't have a built in way to access the EC or control fans.​
​Fun fact:​​ disabling TurboBoost (setting the cpu max power on windows' power management advanced options to 99%) has a perfect pairing on thermals and fan speeds. It really look like Dell (or who for them) draw the fan curve on thermals with TurboBoost disabled.​
​I read about different ways people are "solving" this issue, some are using HWInfo which has a fan management tool that allows you to set a simple table of speeds based on the temperature sensor you choose. It's the only thing that works, and you can even choose the ramp time the fans have to wait before acting, which could be 1ms instead of 5000ms.​
​I don't like it since I'm not an expert in ECs and I don't know if doing this could actually get in the way of the other commands on fans. It does work though, but when setting a fan to Max speed, it won't run as fast as when you leave the system default and get a game to run (you can't see speeds of fans, but based on noise I'm 100% sure of this).​
​Then there's SpeedFan, which doesn't work by default. Opening the options panel and activating the Dell support option seems to do something, since the program manages to retrieve info about fans and speeds, but trying to tweak it will result in fans kicking at the speed you want for the fraction of a second to stop right after, this behaviour repeats in a loop.​
​A user (topic linked below) created an application that disabled EC and allows users to set 3 speeds on fans. This application requires the Testing mode of windows to be enabled, which is something I can't do because 90% of the things I use to work won't allow it.​
​It is clear that this is not a hardware problem, it's just a management thing. Please Dell, provide a solution for us Temps Nerds, a custom fan curve tool, like any other company does would be optimal, but I'd be happy with a simple "super noisy fan mode" too.​
​Some are undervolting their cpus with ThrottleStop, which looks like the last resort to me, undervolting could be fine for you but I bought a high end laptop cpu because I want high end performance, I'd rather get somebody from Dell to provide a proper solution, since I really like my warranty :)​

​6.) Power adapter does not fit snug. It fits as if the end-pint is a bit swollen and will press outward just enough to remove needed contact. Frequently the adapter will not provide proper power to the laptop and must be tinkered with often.​
​Dell support has spent over an hour with me, remoted into my system and the problems are not resolved. The diagnostics from BIOS show no problems. The Windows diagnostics show no OS file corruption. ​While inspecting the issue with HWiNFO, I noticed, that the readings from the TEMP5 temperature sensor on the RTX are erratic. ​Because the sensor works fine, while the computer is AC powered, this seems like a software issue.​

Problems gradually got worse and worse, but when the computer wasn't crashing, it ran well. I learned from a friend that the problem was an intermittently failing RAM stick (or an issue with the motherboard) as it would sometimes recognize 4GB of RAM and sometimes 8GB.​
​Fast forward to the almost a year of owning the computer. Problems are terrible at this point and after my 3rd or 4th contact with support, I finally send the computer in with a comprehensive list of issues I had with it. I wanted to send it in while it was ​​still under warrant​​y, so even though it would cost me a lot of grief in not having my computer (which wasn't cheap mind you), I needed a resolution. Dell seems to forget that customers have lives too and expect quality and reliability in the items we purchase.​

You should fire half of your incompetent service techs and maybe consider hiring some workers for a thing most companies have, quality control. You should have replaced this thing the first time I asked, no consideration at all. Now, it's out of warranty, and it's my problem, right? That's what companies hope for. ​I got a Dell G5 15 5500 (i7, 16GB, RTX 2060) about a year ago. I use it for work and day-to-day use, and occasional gaming (nothing a day one Xbox One couldn't run). It's generally good, but my one big gripe with it is the fan noise.​
​Fair enough it's a reasonably powerful laptop and needs cooling (and I haven't actually had over-heating problems) but the fact that it's loud, near-constant, and high pitched means it's just a headache to use day-to-day, and enjoyable gaming requires either ANC headphones or cables running through to a different room. If you're reading this, you probably already know this for yourself.​
​Here's my top tips for other owners after a year of trying to get it to shut up. I'll mostly talk about getting the fan speed down during day-to-day use, but there are obvious implications for temperatures under high loads.​
​1. Check the drivers from Dell are up to date. I don't have personal experience of this making a difference, but it's the first bit of advice everywhere else. ​
​2. Power profiles and charging. By default you can't delve much into the power profile settings; Windows Settings let you change things like sleep and screen saver timers, and My Dell lets you pick charging speed. Fan speeds will increase if it's charging during use. By default, clock speeds are reduced when it's unplugged, and fan speeds are often noticeably reduced. This can be useful if I'm making a recording and don't want fan noise.​
​3. Thermal profiles and fan curves. There are lots of other posts where you can read about these in detail. They do a bit, but control is limited. For day-to-day use I haven't noticed any difference in performance (clock speed) for thermal profiles, though they're described as balancing performance, noise and temperature. I haven't tested whether they make a difference at high loads. Ironically, the Quite profile is the loudest (other than G-mode). I generally leave it on Balanced. The fan will often run at 40-60% after start-up, and I have to switch between thermal profiles before it will act "normally". ​
​4. Cooling pads. I bought a cooling pad. The only time it's overheated was before I got this. The biggest difference actually just comes from the extra space under the laptop. For day-to-day use I leave the pad fan turned off, and this still noticeably reduces fan speeds. I also get noticeable fan speed reductions by putting the stand at an angle. For day-to-day use the cooling pad fan reduces fan speed, but overall the combined volume is about the same. For high loads I turn the fan on to keep temperatures down. ​
​5. GPU selection. The fan is particularly annoying when I'm in video calls. By default the computer uses the integrated GPU (Intel UHD Graphics) not the dedicated GPU (Nvidia GeForce RTX 2060) for most non-game applications. Using Nvidia Control Panel to set the preferred processor to the GPU instead of the CPU for programs like Zoom and Chrome seems to spread the heat and reduce fan speeds. ​
​6. Desk fan. Externally, it's noticeable that the bit of the laptop that gets hottest is the top of the laptop above the keyboard. The laptop and pad fans blow air onto the bottom and through the radiator out the back, but don't remove heat from the top of the laptop. For desk use, I've started pointing a desk fan at the laptop. This probably makes the single biggest difference other than not leaving it on a flat surface (passive cooling pad). Even if it's not always quieter, the lower pitch of the desk fan strains my ears less. ​
​If you have any tips to share, let me know!​

Titulo_Post: Inspiron G5 15 5500, weak link Nvidia chipset and driver
Conteudo_Post:
​Not that the chipset is bad mind you; its decent... but its been a pain in the neck; for everyone... artists, gamers, developers -- name it. ​
​I started getting raster noise, lower screen flickering (especially in Win32 API graphics in motion, horizontal) and it was so hardware-like I immediately suspected the monitor! No, three monitors later I confirmed it was the NVidia driver & or chipset. I ended up having to reload the NVidia driver completely. Then what driver to use (studio, or gaming?)​
​There isn't a hill of beans difference between the two drivers (unless you're using two or three special purpose artsie fartsie apps)... if you're not sure, use the gaming driver (works great for both).​
​Also a quick note, probably common knowledge for Dell techies, the internal display LCD of the G5 5500 is NOT on the NVidia chipset GTX 1660 Ti ! The internal display (UHD) in on the embedded Intel Graphics Chipset ! This is the main reason the strange behaviors of your external monitor are quite different from the on-board LCD (completely different chipset, driver).​
​According to bing, flickering in Win10 means reload your graphics driver; I can confirm. I know this sounds a bit extreme (and I agree) but something gets honked up between the system, the GPU chipset, and the G driver... that can only be resolved by completely reloading the NVidia driver... take the option for custom install, and then select the option for Clean Install. This will fix the annoying Win10 video flickering problems on your external monitor.​
​So far, I have not had any issues with the Intel Graphics chipset, generic driver, nor internal LCD.​

Titulo_Post: Dell G5 15 5587 unusual CPU-Usage with workaround
Conteudo_Post: ​Hi everyone!​​I am experiencing a bug, which followed me for quite some time.​​On usual settings in windows 10, I experienced that even common windows tasks make the system seem laggy. Then I checked the ressource-monitor to see that CPU0, the first logical processor-core is stuck at 100% usage. After some testing I found, that after deactivating Intel PCI-Express Root Port #14 - A335, the processor usage went down and behaved normally. I believe this root port is connected to the internal network-adapter, since disabling it, the network-interface disappears aswell. After several Firmware updates didn't fix the issure, I wanted to share this behaviour with you. Since I am never using the internal LAN-interface I am not too concerned, but still.​​For everyone who uses this Laptop with Windows 10, you might want to check if this happens to you aswell. Just open up the Ressource Monitor and check if one Core is constantly at 100% and if so, try disabling one the of the PCI-Express Root ports and check again. This shouldn't break anything major and you can revert the setting afterwards.​​For Dell I'd hope to have something check this behaviour and maybe fix it in one of the next firmware updates. I don't use any software related to the killer-network-interface which might cause this problem.​​Best regards,​​Alex​
